records.decision_reason: The paper independently compares human, GPT-5, and Gemini inductive code trees and then tests all three against the same human codebook on a stratified subsample.

Research objective.value: Compare GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro with human qualitative coding of Dutch newspaper coverage of nurses during COVID-19.
Research objective.anchor: To what extent can GPT-5 and Gemini

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Comparative qualitative content analysis using open, axial, and selective coding.
Claimed qualitative methodology.anchor: The human analysis proceeded in 3 iterative steps

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Two humans built a consensus inductive coding tree on all 317 articles; GPT-5 and Gemini independently built model-optimized coding trees; all three then applied the human codebook to 31 stratified articles in article-by-article sessions.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid: independent inductive code-tree generation followed by deductive codebook application

Domain.value: nursing and health-services media discourse during COVID-19 in Limburg, Netherlands

Dataset name.value: De Limburger articles retrieved from Nexis Uni, 2020–2023
Dataset name.anchor: The data for this study consist of newspaper articles

Public or restricted data.value: licensed newspaper corpus from Nexis Uni; not reported as publicly released

Number of documents.value: 317 articles; 31 in the deductive validation subsample

Language.value: Dutch source articles; coding labels produced in English
Language.anchor: Although the dataset consisted of Dutch articles

Exact model/version.value: GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro via consumer web interfaces; exact snapshots and sampling parameters not exposed

Prompting strategy.value: Model-specific self-optimized prompts; full-corpus iterative induction; revised codebook and article-by-article deductive coding after a GPT-5 pilot exposed overbroad coding and omissions.

Human role.value: Two researchers created and reconciled the human codebook, validated the baseline, refined prompts/code definitions, transferred model codes, and interpreted divergence.

Unit of analysis.value: meaningful quoted text segment within an article
Unit of analysis.anchor: unit of analysis was the coded quotation

Generated outputs.value: Three inductive coding trees and deductive code assignments for 31 articles

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Article-by-article outputs, verbatim coded sentences, coding-tree supplements, and merged ATLAS.ti projects for the human reliability check

Baselines.value: Consensus human codebook and independently double-coded human subsample

Number of runs or seeds.value: One continuous induction session per model and two deductive protocol rounds for GPT-5; no stochastic reruns
Number of runs or seeds.anchor: single, continuous chat session per model

Human-evaluation design.value: Two independent humans coded the 31-article subsample; human-model code applications were compared using the same codebook and overlap settings.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: Two researchers; degrees and affiliations reported, qualitative-coding experience not fully characterized

Inter-rater reliability.value: human-human α=0.703; human-GPT-5 α=0.487; human-Gemini α=0.507

Principal results.value: Both models found plausible high-level themes but applied 181/183 codes versus the human's 138; low human-model alpha and qualitative review indicated systematic overcoding and a semantic-presence versus interpretive-significance difference.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Maastricht University ethics approval was reported; licensed Dutch newspaper texts were uploaded through consumer model interfaces under institutional governance.

Reproducibility resources.value: Full prompts and coding trees/codebooks are supplied in the multimedia appendix; provider snapshots and executable code are not reported.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report one regional Dutch source, model/version and prompt dependence, consumer-interface opacity, context/omission problems, and limited generalizability to other languages and qualitative tasks.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: the human baseline was developed by researchers already familiar with the corpus, whereas model prompts were optimized separately; alpha measures application concordance, not which divergent interpretation is substantively better.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: prior exposure can introduce blind spots

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Direct evidence that high-level theme overlap can conceal systematic overcoding and low decision-level agreement; supports trace-level comparison and prompt/run audits.

records.decision_reason: The study compares independently generated human and GPT-5.2 codebooks on the same 200-response corpus, with blinded dual application and chance-corrected reliability analysis.

Research objective.value: Compare the usability and inter-coder reliability of human-derived and AI-derived thematic codebooks for surgical survey responses.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Inductive thematic analysis and codebook comparison.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Two researchers iteratively created a human codebook; GPT-5.2 generated a codebook from the same 200 responses with one zero-shot prompt; the same two blinded coders then independently applied each finalized codebook in a binary multi-label design.
Actual operationalized methodology.anchor: The same dataset of 200 responses was input

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: hybrid: inductive codebook generation followed by deductive application

Domain.value: barriers to laparoscopic common bile duct exploration in surgical practice

Public or restricted data.value: de-identified secondary survey data; public release not reported

Number of documents.anchor: A total of 200 open-ended survey responses

Approximate corpus size.value: 200 short responses to one open-ended survey question

Prompting strategy.value: One disclosed zero-shot request to create a multi-label thematic codebook; default parameters, one batch, no iterative refinement

Human role.value: Two authors created the human codebook, independently applied both codebooks while blinded to each other's assignments, and reached consensus on structured qualitative comparison.

Unit of analysis.value: open-ended survey response; meaningful text segment for code assignment

Generated outputs.value: Two 13-code codebooks and binary multi-label assignments under each
Generated outputs.anchor: Both the HC and AIC independently produced 13 codes

Baselines.value: Independently created human codebook on the identical corpus

Number of runs or seeds.value: one GPT-5.2 generation; 1,000 bootstrap resamples for uncertainty, not model stability

Automatic metrics.value: percent agreement, Cohen's kappa, Gwet's AC1, bootstrap confidence intervals, and Δκ

Human-evaluation design.value: Within-coder comparison: the same two coders independently applied both codebooks; structured qualitative comparison covered separation, overlap, ease, and ambiguity.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: two study authors/coders; detailed qualitative expertise not reported

Statistical analysis.value: Paired nonparametric bootstrap with 1,000 resamples and code-level agreement analysis in RStudio

Principal results.value: Both codebooks found 13 codes and shared five explicit barriers, but the human codebook yielded higher reliability and clearer boundaries; the AI codebook was broader and more overlapping.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Wake Forest School of Medicine IRB approval for the de-identified secondary dataset

Reproducibility resources.value: The exact generation prompt and analysis formulas are reported; data/code availability and model snapshot are not reported.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report same-coder familiarity/carryover, only 200 short responses, one model and one prompt, no repeated generations or prompt sensitivity, and evaluation limited to early codebook usability rather than full interpretive quality.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: reusing the human-codebook developers to apply both codebooks creates asymmetric familiarity; higher application reliability does not by itself establish a truer interpretation.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: does not aim to equate higher inter-coder reliability

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Strong design warning about separating codebook generation quality, code application reliability, rater familiarity, and interpretive validity.

records.decision_reason: AutoTheme implements autonomous multi-agent inductive coding and theme reconciliation on app reviews, with an LDA comparator and disclosed agent prompts.

Research objective.value: Develop an agentic framework for inductive thematic analysis of short text with minimal human intervention.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Two GPT-4.1 coder agents independently coded reviews, a third reconciled codes, two theme agents grouped consolidated codes, and a theme-reconciler agent merged their theme sets; outputs were descriptively compared with LDA/PyLDAVis topics labeled by two humans.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive within a prompt-constrained functional-feature scope

Domain.value: consumer reviews of cognitive-behavioral-therapy mobile applications

Number of documents.value: 24,902 four- and five-star reviews collected; only the successfully coded subset counts are reported for agent stages

Exact model/version.value: GPT-4.1 through the OpenAI Agents SDK; snapshot and parameters not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Role-specific disclosed prompts constrain initial codes to explicitly mentioned functional features, then reconcile two code lists and two independently generated theme sets.

Single-agent or multi-agent.anchor: initial coding process consists of three agents

Agent roles.value: two independent coder agents; code reconciler; two theme-generator agents; theme reconciler

Human role.value: Researchers set the analytic scope and compare outputs; two independent researchers label LDA topics; no human validation of individual agent codes is reported.
Human role.anchor: LDA results were labeled by two independent

Generated outputs.value: review-level codes and reconciled design-feature themes

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: The pipeline retains code-to-review processing artifacts and sample coded reviews, but a complete source-to-theme audit package is not reported.
Evidence/provenance mechanism.anchor: Appendix A shows sample coded reviews

Baselines.value: LDA topic modeling with PyLDAVis, human-labeled by two researchers
Baselines.anchor: compared to a set of themes generated using Latent Dirichlet

Number of runs or seeds.value: one reported multi-agent execution; repeated model runs/seeds not reported

Automatic metrics.value: descriptive counts of coded reviews and themes; no validated theme-quality metric

Human-evaluation design.value: Descriptive researcher comparison against human-labeled LDA topics; no blinded independent qualitative evaluation

Principal results.value: The reconciliation agents produced 10 final design-feature themes versus six LDA themes and were described as more detailed; evidence is descriptive rather than a formal superiority test.
Principal results.anchor: identified a total of 10 design feature themes

Reproducibility resources.value: Role prompts and architecture are printed; a Streamlit implementation is described, but repository, exact snapshot, seeds, and complete outputs are not reported.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report the single domain, restriction to positive short reviews, LDA-only comparator, prompt dependence, and need for comparisons with human thematic analysis and other datasets/models.
Author-reported limitations.anchor: This work is not without limitations

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: multiple agents share one underlying model and prompt framing, so reconciliation is not independent triangulation; more/finer themes than LDA do not establish interpretive validity.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Useful agent-role and reconciliation baseline, but highlights the need for source-level auditing and independent human evaluation.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access journal article in Dementia, first published online 2026
records.decision_reason: The study uses a human–LLM parallel code set and compares code-domain concordance, while clearly retaining human thematic interpretation as the reference.

Research objective.value: Describe Malaysian family caregivers' dementia-care burden, support gaps, and service priorities.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Phenomenological thematic interpretation plus structured content analysis with parallel human and LLM coding.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: An experienced qualitative researcher iteratively created a prespecified codebook; a fine-tuned but unspecified LLM applied the same labels; major-domain presence/absence was compared on a subset, and the human-coded data remained primary.
Actual operationalized methodology.anchor: Two parallel code sets were generated

Domain.value: dementia caregiving and service/workforce needs in Malaysia

Document length.value: interviews approximately 30 minutes to 2 hours; no audio recording
Document length.anchor: ranged from approximately 30 minutes to 2 hours

Language.anchor: communicate in Malay, English, or Tamil

Model family.value: large language model; provider/family not reported

Fine-tuning or adaptation.value: reported as fine-tuned to apply the human code labels; procedure, training data, and parameters not reported
Fine-tuning or adaptation.anchor: fine-tuned to apply the same code labels

Human role.value: Two experienced interviewers collected data; an experienced qualitative researcher developed codes; humans retained all interpretation and final thematic coding.
Human role.anchor: all interpretations, conclusions, and final thematic coding

Unit of analysis.value: free-text answer to six core open-ended interview questions
Unit of analysis.anchor: focus is on six core open-ended questions

Generated outputs.value: parallel human and machine code files and human-led themes of emotional, financial, informational, and service burden

Baselines.value: experienced human coder as the primary analytic reference
Baselines.anchor: human interpretation was retained as the primary

Automatic metrics.value: descriptive domain frequencies; qualitative statement of high concordance, with no coefficient or contingency table reported

Human-evaluation design.value: Human–LLM major-domain comparison on an unspecified subset; discrepancies reviewed for granularity/direction
Human-evaluation design.anchor: compared with human expert codes in a subset

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: one experienced qualitative researcher in dementia/caregiving as reference; two clinically/research-experienced interviewers

Inter-rater reliability.value: not reported; concordance characterized qualitatively as high

Principal results.value: Core burden domains were directionally robust across coder types; the LLM collapsed nuanced emotional language and missed culturally specific expressions and sarcasm, so results relied on human coding.
Principal results.anchor: limitations in capturing culturally specific expressions

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Malaysian MREC approval NMRR ID 24-03509-R1K; written consent, distress safeguards, de-identification, and restricted data

Reproducibility resources.value: Human_codes_full.csv and AI_codes_full.csv are named but not made public; model, tuning procedure, prompts, and concordance sample are not reported.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report a single public site, family-caregiver-only perspective, interim 67-person cutoff, and predominantly female sample.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: absent model/prompt/tuning details, unspecified validation subset, and no numeric agreement make the computational comparison nonreproducible and weak as validation evidence.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: most discrepancies reflecting differences in granularity

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Shows why domain-level concordance should not substitute for trace-level evaluation of cultural nuance, sarcasm, and code granularity.

records.decision_reason: The full article compares human immersion–crystallization analysis with ChatGPT 4.0 theme generation on the same two surgical applicant datasets.

Research objective.value: Assess whether ChatGPT can replicate human qualitative analysis of surgery-applicant wellness and engagement responses.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Human immersion–crystallization qualitative analysis compared with AI thematic analysis.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Researchers used immersion–crystallization to produce themes for two free-text datasets; a single ChatGPT-4.0 prompt independently requested four themes per dataset; authors visually mapped conceptual overlap.
Actual operationalized methodology.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, qualitative-analysis comparison

Domain.value: general-surgery residency applicant wellness and program engagement
Domain.anchor: official HTML full text, Study population

Number of documents.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, n=117

Number of participants.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, 117 applicants

Model family.anchor: official HTML full text, ChatGPT analysis

Exact model/version.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, ChatGPT 4.0

Prompting strategy.value: single prompt requesting four themes for each complete dataset; no iterative refinement or rerun
Prompting strategy.anchor: official HTML full text, Methods, single-prompt procedure

Human role.value: Researchers conducted the human analysis and descriptively mapped human and model themes.

Unit of analysis.anchor: official HTML full text, Data collection

Generated outputs.value: four human and four ChatGPT themes per dataset

Human-evaluation design.value: Author comparison of thematic maps; independent blinded raters and formal scoring rubric not reported

Principal results.value: Human and model analyses shared broad concepts, and the model produced no unique or contradictory theme; the comparison did not quantify trace-level agreement or nuance.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors note two short datasets from one applicant cohort, one model/prompt, and the descriptive nature of comparison.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: forcing exactly four themes and visually matching broad concepts can inflate apparent agreement; a single run and no source-level coding comparison cannot establish replication.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Negative-control example showing that apparent high-level agreement can arise under coarse, same-cardinality theme matching without trace-level validation.

records.publication_status_as_of_cutoff: peer-reviewed open-access case study in Online Journal of Public Health Informatics, 2026
records.decision_reason: The paper compares ChatGPT-4 with human thematic analysis on four public-health text subsets using an explicit proficiency/reasonableness rubric, alongside sentiment and topic tasks.

Research objective.value: Evaluate accessible NLP/LLM tools against human coding for sentiment, topic, and thematic analysis of Australian COVID-19 public-health discourse.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: Braun and Clarke six-step thematic analysis plus sentiment and topic analysis.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Google Alerts articles and X posts were screened; one human and zero-shot ChatGPT-4 independently produced thematic analyses for four positive/negative subsets; model themes were cross-matched to human themes and rated for proficiency and reasonableness.

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.value: inductive thematic analysis; sentiment classification is deductive

Domain.value: Australian public opinion about COVID-19 mitigation measures

Dataset name.value: Google Alerts and X public-health-measures corpus, December 2022–February 2023
Dataset name.anchor: Data were collected via Google Alerts

Public or restricted data.value: public web/news and social-media posts, subject to platform access

Number of documents.value: 2,227 Google Alerts records and 3,484 tweets collected; 1,238/2,473 deemed relevant in the abstracted flow; four sentiment subsets used for themes

Model family.value: OpenAI ChatGPT plus VADER, SentimentGI, SentimentQDAP, Microsoft Azure, and LDA

Exact model/version.value: ChatGPT-4; Microsoft Azure Text Analytics 3.1 (2023); exact ChatGPT snapshot not reported

Prompting strategy.value: Zero-shot prompts documented in Multimedia Appendix 1 for sentiment, topic selection, and replication of human thematic analysis

Human role.value: Humans screened relevance, created sentiment guidelines/reference labels, performed topic summaries and thematic analyses, adjudicated sentiment disagreements, and scored model themes.

Unit of analysis.value: news article/search result or X post; theme output scored at theme level

Generated outputs.value: sentiment labels, topic lists, and 20 model-generated thematic outputs across four subsets

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Prompts, code, human/model result tables, and theme-matching rubric in multimedia appendices; source-to-theme quote trail is limited.
Evidence/provenance mechanism.anchor: code is included in Multimedia Appendix 2

Baselines.value: Human sentiment coding, human manual topic summaries, human Braun–Clarke thematic analysis, and LDA

Number of runs or seeds.value: one reported zero-shot ChatGPT run per task/dataset; stochastic repeats not reported

Automatic metrics.value: Cohen kappa for sentiment, percent agreement, confidence intervals; rubric counts for theme proficiency and 0–2 reasonableness

Human-evaluation design.value: A researcher scored each LLM theme against human output for proficiency and independently for reasonableness; sentiment subset double-coded by two humans.

Number and expertise of evaluators.value: two human sentiment raters; thematic-output scoring appears to rely on the research team, with evaluator count/expertise not fully reported
Number and expertise of evaluators.anchor: coded for sentiment by 2 human raters

Inter-rater reliability.value: Cohen κ below 0.5 for every model/tool sentiment comparison; human-human κ reported in supplementary results

Principal results.value: Thirteen of 20 model theme outputs were proficient and seven partially proficient; outputs were coherent at a high level but missed contextual insight, while sentiment tools had poor concordance.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: UNSW Human Research Ethics Committee approval reported; public online content and ChatGPT use described as limited

Reproducibility resources.value: Prompts and analysis code are supplied in multimedia appendices; exact ChatGPT snapshot and repeated-run artifacts are absent.

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors report a short Australian time window, platform/search-selection bias, English-only data, rapidly changing tool versions, subjective theme scoring, and limited generalizability.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: the same human analysis anchors both matching and proficiency judgments, and theme-level reasonableness without source-level audits can miss omissions, distortions, and plausible unsupported synthesis.

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Provides a useful two-axis theme rubric but also demonstrates why reasonableness and overlap require independent evidence-grounding checks.

records.decision_reason: Computational KJ-Hō specifies a highly relevant proposed architecture and evaluation plan, but repeatedly identifies itself as a concept paper whose CPT/SFT implementation and metrics remain for later empirical validation.

Research objective.value: Propose a domain-specialized computational realization of the Japanese KJ method for large-scale consumer insight extraction and strategy generation.

Claimed qualitative methodology.value: KJ method integrated with grounded theory and abductive reasoning.

Actual operationalized methodology.value: Conceptual three-layer architecture: CPT on a marketing corpus, SFT on expert-curated insight pairs, bottom-up embedding/clustering, evidence-linked insight generation, strategy generation, and planned human/metric evaluation; the target system is not yet empirically implemented.
Actual operationalized methodology.anchor: This paper is a concept paper

Inductive, deductive, or hybrid.anchor: without referring to a predefined category system

Domain.value: Japanese marketing research and consumer psychology

Fine-tuning or adaptation.value: proposed continued pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning on mutually reviewed expert pairs

Single-agent or multi-agent.value: single domain-specialized pipeline; planned comparator groups

Human role.value: Humans define objectives, mutually curate SFT data, supervise, audit evidence links, judge outputs, and make strategic decisions.
Human role.anchor: human analyst defines the marketing-research objective

Generated outputs.value: proposed bottom-up clusters, evidence-linked insight headings, and strategy recommendations

Evidence/provenance mechanism.value: Architecture requires each insight to link explicitly to supporting data for audit; not empirically demonstrated.
Evidence/provenance mechanism.anchor: explicit evidence link to its supporting data

Baselines.value: planned general-purpose LLM, CPT-only, CPT+SFT, and independent human-team comparisons

Automatic metrics.value: proposed InsightExtraction-F1 and MarketingQA; target/thresholds are normative, not established results
Automatic metrics.anchor: normative goal rather than an empirically established

Human-evaluation design.value: planned blinded expert ratings of validity, usefulness, and novelty against independent human analyses

Principal results.value: No completed system evaluation is reported; two cited/preliminary Japanese studies motivate the design but are not an evaluation of the proposed CPT+SFT framework.

Efficiency or cost results.value: A roughly one-tenth self-hosting cost is projected, not measured in this study.

Ethics and privacy treatment.value: Conceptual discussion covers data sovereignty, automation bias, Western/WEIRD bias, human oversight, and transparency.

Reproducibility resources.value: No implemented model, corpus, benchmark, prompts, or code released with the concept paper.
Reproducibility resources.anchor: will be reported in this study's

Author-reported limitations.value: Authors acknowledge concept-stage status, text-only scope, domain-specific transfer limits, large training-data demands, unvalidated proposed metrics, automation bias, and unresolved trust calibration.

Additional validity concerns.value: Reviewer concern: 'analyst-bias-free' is an overclaim for a pipeline whose corpus curation, expert SFT pairs, clustering criteria, and evaluation gold standards all embed human and model assumptions; no empirical evidence yet supports bias reduction.
Additional validity concerns.anchor: should be understood as a methodology that structurally reduces analyst bias

Relevance to the proposed ARR project.value: Contextual source for evidence-linked insight design, non-Western methodology, ablations, and the distinction between proposed and empirically validated metrics.
